hook: Write report sentences the way German offices do: wegen fehlender Unterlagen instead of a whole weil-clause.
intro: A formal report (Bericht) in German, whether from a municipal department, a company or a project team, is written largely in nominal style: instead of subordinate clauses with weil, nachdem, um … zu or obwohl, it uses a preposition plus a noun phrase. Weil Unterlagen fehlten becomes wegen fehlender Unterlagen, nachdem die Leitungen erneuert worden waren becomes nach Erneuerung der Leitungen, um die Kosten zu senken becomes zur Senkung der Kosten. The text becomes shorter, more impersonal and denser, which is exactly the register readers expect in reports, statements and formal e-mails. The skill is choosing the right preposition for the relation (cause, time, purpose, concession, condition), the right noun for the verb, and the right case: most of these prepositions take the genitive, and an adjective without an article must show the case itself (fehlender, starker, weiterer). This quiz walks through one coherent interim report on the renovation of a street; each draft sentence is followed by its nominal version with the decisive phrase missing.
tips[0].title: Cause, concession, condition
tips[0].text: weil → wegen / aufgrund / infolge + Gen; obwohl → trotz / ungeachtet + Gen; wenn / falls → bei + Dat or im Falle + Gen.
tips[0].trap: Without an article the adjective carries the genitive ending: wegen fehlender Unterlagen, trotz starker Regenfälle. Mangels takes a bare noun (mangels Unterlagen).
tips[0].check.why: obwohl expresses a concession, so it becomes trotz + Genitiv; wegen and infolge would turn it into a cause.
tips[1].title: Time: vor, nach, während, bei
tips[1].text: bevor → vor + Dat; nachdem → nach + Dat; während / solange → während + Gen or für die Dauer + Gen; als (once) → bei + Dat.
tips[1].check.why: nachdem (after) becomes nach + Dativ; vor would replace bevor.
tips[2].title: Purpose: zur / zum + noun
tips[2].text: um … zu / damit → zu + Dat (zur Senkung, zum Schutz) or zwecks + noun without article. The object of the verb becomes a genitive attribute.
tips[2].check.why: Purpose becomes zu + Dativ, and der Schutz is masculine: zu dem → zum Schutz.
tips[3].title: Don’t overdo it
tips[3].text: A good report mixes nominal phrases with ordinary verbs. Two or three nominal chains per paragraph are enough; a sentence with four genitives in a row is hard to read and loses the reader.
tips[3].check.why: It mixes one nominal phrase with an ordinary verb; the second piles up genitives, the third is chatty and not report style.
table.caption: Verbal style → nominal style in reports
remember[0]: Choose the preposition for the relation first: wegen/aufgrund (cause), trotz (concession), bei/im Falle (condition), vor/nach/während (time), zur/zum (purpose).
remember[1]: The verb’s object becomes a genitive: die Kosten senken → die Senkung der Kosten.
remember[2]: No article → the adjective shows the case: wegen fehlender Unterlagen, trotz starker Regenfälle.
exam: Nominal style shows the formal register the C1 exam's writing asks for — and it is how offices and companies actually write reports.
mistakes[0].why: Without an article the adjective takes the strong genitive plural ending -er.
mistakes[1].why: The object of the verb becomes a genitive attribute of the noun.
mistakes[2].why: nach takes the dative; in reports the article is often dropped.
